# The Core Four — The Advertising Engine

**Source:** *$100M Leads*, Section III "Get Leads: The Core Four Advertising Methods" (lines ~925–2710)
+ the Rule of 100 (l.2792–2826). This is the heart of the Leads engine. The four channel sub-skills —
`hormozi-lead-warm`, `hormozi-lead-content`, `hormozi-lead-cold`, `hormozi-lead-paid` — each read their
own section below.

The Core Four are **the only four ways one person can let other people know about anything** (l.947).
Everything else (lead getters, automation) is these four, scaled. You either do them "with enough skill
or with enough volume" or get out-advertised (l.961).

---

## Overview — the 2×2 that defines the Core Four

Two axes (l.929–955):

- **Audience:** **Warm** = "people who gave you permission to contact you" (friends, family, followers,
  customers) vs. **Cold** = "people who have not given you permission" (strangers, other people's
  audiences) (l.933–935).
- **Communication:** **1-to-1 / private** (phone call, email — one person at a time) vs.
  **1-to-many / public** (social post, billboard, podcast — many at once) (l.939–941). Automation just
  means a machine does some of the work; the *nature* of the communication is unchanged (l.943).

Crossing them gives the Core Four (l.949–955):

| | Warm (knows you) | Cold (stranger) |
|---|---|---|
| **1-to-1 (private)** | **Warm Outreach** | **Cold Outreach** |
| **1-to-many (public)** | **Post Free Content** | **Paid Ads** |

Recommended learning order (skills transfer forward, and paid ads cost the money the others earn):
**Warm Outreach → Post Free Content → Cold Outreach → Paid Ads** (l.2706, l.2766). In every channel you
advertise the *same* two things: your **lead magnet** (free/low-cost) or your **core offer** (l.1007).

---

## The Rule of 100 (the volume law across all four)

**"You advertise your stuff by doing 100 primary actions every day, for one hundred days in a row."**
(l.2794) Do that and you *will* get more engaged leads — the one promise the book makes. Applied per
channel (l.2798–2826):

- **Warm Outreach:** **100 reach outs/day** (email, text, DM, calls).
- **Post Content:** **100 minutes/day making content**; release **≥1 piece/day** per platform (post
  more as you improve).
- **Cold Outreach:** **100 reach outs/day** (email, text, DM, cold call, flyers); expect lower response
  rates, so use automation.
- **Paid Ads:** **100 minutes/day making ads**, run for **100 days straight** on the daily budget from
  the paid-ads math; aim for Client-Financed Acquisition.

Measure inputs (you control them); outputs follow with consistency.

## Warm Outreach

*(1-to-1 to a warm audience. Read by `hormozi-lead-warm`.)*

**How it works (l.1003–1011):** one-to-one contact with people who already know you — calls, texts,
emails, DMs, voicemails. Cheapest and easiest way to find interested people, and most businesses skip
it. You *do* have a warm audience even if you think you don't ("everybody knows somebody"). Low yield
per hour but **reliable** — "as certain as the sun rises and sets, it works" (l.1009).

### The 10 Steps (l.1017–1035) — get your "First Five Clients"

1. **Get your list** — everyone has one. Add up every contact across phone, all your email accounts,
   and every social platform; that's often your first ~1,000 leads (l.1037–1047).
2. **Pick a platform** — start with the one where you have the *most* contacts; you'll hit them all
   eventually (l.1051).
3. **Personalize your greeting** — open with something you actually know about them (check their
   profile if needed); you haven't asked for anything, so relax. *Pattern:* "*Saw you just had a baby!
   Congrats! How's the baby?*" (l.1055–1061).
4. **Reach out — to 100 people every day** (l.1063). Contact each **up to 3 times: once per day for 3
   days or until they respond** (physical mail: once per week) (l.1069–1071).
5. **Warm them up with the A-C-A framework** when they reply (l.1077–1095):
   - **Acknowledge** — restate what they said in your words (active listening).
   - **Compliment** — tie it to a positive character trait.
   - **Ask another question** — steer toward a topic closer to your offer (e.g. fitness: "*Do you have
     time to get workouts in?*").
6. **Invite their friends / make the offer** — after ~3–4 exchanges (or 3–4 min in person), make an
   offer to test interest, built on the **Value Equation** (Dream Outcome, Perceived Likelihood of
   Achievement, Time Delay, Effort & Sacrifice — maximize the first two, minimize the last two;
   l.1103–1121). *Script pattern* (l.1135): "*…do you know anybody who is [struggle] looking to [dream
   outcome] in [time delay]? I'm taking on five case studies for free… I help them [dream outcome]
   without [effort & sacrifice]… I even guarantee [dream outcome] or I work with them until they do…
   Does anyone come to mind?*" — key move: **you ask if they know anyone, not if they'll buy**, which
   removes pushiness and lets them self-select (l.1137). Compressed one-liner (l.1141): "*I help [ideal
   customer] get [dream outcome] in [time period] without [effort & sacrifice] and [perceived
   likelihood booster].*"
7. **Make them the easiest offer in the world — make it free** (l.1145–1179). *Script pattern* (l.1151):
   "*Since I'm only taking on five people… I'll give it all for free so long as you promise to: 1) Use
   it 2) Give me feedback 3) Leave a killer review if it deserves one. Sound fair?*" Make the **first
   five free** (the exact number matters less than the reason): you get reps, you're forgiven while you
   "suck," you learn fast, and value delivered → reviews, feedback, referrals. Free customers pay off 3
   ways: convert to paying, refer paying customers, and their testimonials sell (l.1171–1179).
   - **If they say no → ask why** (l.1181–1193). The real cost is the **hidden costs** (time, effort,
     sacrifice = the bottom of the Value Equation). Ask: "*What would I have to do to make it worth it
     for you to continue?*" Their answer either wins them or arms you for the next person.
8. **Start at the top** — when one platform is exhausted, move to the platform with the next-most
   contacts, and so on (l.1195–1201).
9. **Start charging** — the litmus test: **once people start referring, start charging** (l.1205).
   Swap "*free*" → "*80% off* for the next five," then 60%, 40%… raising ~20% every five (this also
   adds real urgency because prices actually rise) (l.1207).
10. **Keep your list warm** — give regular value (email, content) so the list stays primed. Probe it
    with Dean Jackson's **9-word email**: "*Are you still looking to [4-word desire]?*" — no images, no
    links, just the question; replies are your top-priority reach-outs (l.1209–1229).

### Benchmarks (l.1237–1257)

- ~**1 in 5** contacts engage → **100 reach outs ≈ 20 replies** (l.1239).
- ~**1 in 5** of those take the free offer → **~4 people** (l.1239).
- ~**1 of those 4** converts to paid later → **~1 customer per 100 reach outs** (l.1239–1241).
- **$100k/yr on warm outreach alone:** assume 1% of list buys a **$400** offer → **500 reach
  outs/week = 5 customers/week** → 5 × $400 = **$2,000/wk** → × 52 = **$104,000/yr** (l.1243–1253).
- Time floor when starting: **~4 hours/day minimum**, first thing each morning (l.1263).

### Output contract for `hormozi-lead-warm`
The assembled contact list + chosen platform; the personalized-greeting opener; the A-C-A reply
skeleton; the filled-in offer script (Value-Equation blanks completed for *this* product) and the
free-offer script; the charging ladder; and the 9-word re-engagement email — all in the product's voice,
with any numbers as real economics or `<placeholder>`.

## Post Free Content

*(1-to-many to a warm audience. Read by `hormozi-lead-content`.)*

**How it works (l.1349–1367):** say it once, reach many. People who find it valuable join your warm
audience; if they think others will value it, they share, and *those* people join too — the audience is
the compounding asset, not the content (l.1333). Free content also makes **every other advertising
method more effective** (l.1359). Trade-offs: harder to personalize, you compete with everyone, and
success invites copycats (l.1363).

### The Content Unit — 3 components (l.1369–1391)

The smallest material that can **Hook · Retain · Reward** attention is one **content unit** (can be a
single image, meme, or sentence doing all three at once). Longer content = many units linked (l.1551).

**1) Hook — get them to notice it** (l.1393–1487). Measured by the % who *start* consuming. Three levers:
- **Topics** — 5 categories (l.1399–1435): **Far Past** (old life lessons tied to your product),
  **Recent Past** (do stuff, then talk about it — meetings, calls, testimonials/case studies),
  **Present** (capture ideas the moment they hit; post them), **Trending** (go where attention is, add
  your angle), **Manufactured** (create the experience, then show it — costliest, biggest payoff).
- **Headlines** — from a meta-analysis of news; **include at least two** (l.1437–1475): **Recency**,
  **Relevancy** (personally meaningful), **Celebrity** (prominent people/authorities), **Proximity**
  (close to home), **Conflict** (opposing ideas/people), **Unusual** (odd/rare/bizarre), **Ongoing**
  (still-unfolding stories).
- **Format** — match the platform's popular format first, then tweak to hook your ideal audience
  (l.1477–1485).

**2) Retain — get them to consume it** (l.1489–1523). Driver = **curiosity**; embed unresolved
questions via three structures:
- **Lists** — themed items ("Top 10 Mistakes"); flexible, less explicit reward.
- **Steps** — ordered actions to a goal; less flexible, more explicit reward.
- **Stories** — real or imagined; people want to know what happens next.
- Interweave them (lists within steps, a story per item) freely.

**3) Reward — satisfy the reason they consumed** (l.1525–1547). Think **value per second**: "there is
no such thing as too long, only too boring" (l.1527). You can't guarantee a reward, but you raise its
odds by hooking the *right* audience, retaining with lists/steps/stories, and clearly answering the
embedded questions. The audience decides — **you know you rewarded them if your audience grows** (l.1543).

### Give : Ask ratio (l.1571–1587)

Gary Vaynerchuk's "jab, jab, jab, right hook" — deposit goodwill with gives, then withdraw with an ask.
Benchmarks: TV runs ~**13 min ads / 60 min = ~3.5 : 1** give:ask; Facebook ~**4 posts : 1 ad** (l.1575).
Those are *mature, maximally-monetizing* ratios; **growing** platforms give far more. Best strategy:
**"Give until they ask"** — give so much people come to *you* (DM, email, site) to buy; **give in
public, ask in private** (l.1579–1583).

### How to make money from content: Ask (l.1589–1619)

Two ways to weave in the ask (each = advertise your **core offer** *or* your **lead magnet**):
- **Integrated** — an ask in most pieces, but keep the give:ask ratio high (e.g. an hour podcast with
  3×30-sec ads = 58.5 min give / 1.5 min ask) (l.1595–1597).
- **Intermittent** — many pure "give" pieces, then an occasional "ask" piece (e.g. 10 gives, 11th
  promotes) (l.1603).
- Rule of thumb: short-form platforms favor **intermittent**; long-form favor **integrated** (l.1605).
  If unsure which offer to run, **use the lead magnet — lower risk** (l.1619). *Offer script* (l.1613):
  "*I'm looking for 5 [avatar] to help achieve [dream outcome] in [time delay]… and if you don't get
  [dream outcome] I'll 1) hand your money back 2) work with you until you do… if that sounds fair,
  DM me / book a call / comment / reply.*"

### How to scale it (l.1621–1663)

Two valid approaches:
- **Depth then width** — maximize one platform (up to ~10 short posts/day, or ~5 days/week long-form),
  *then* add the next. Compounds fastest, fewer resources; risk = single-channel dependence.
- **Width then depth** — get on every relevant platform early, then maximize together. Broader reach +
  repurposing efficiency; costs more labor and risks "sucky fluff everywhere."

### The 7 content lessons (l.1681–1705)

1. **Switch "How to" → "How I"** (share experience; it's unquestionable).
2. **We need to be reminded more than taught** (repeat yourself — most of your audience misses most
   posts; 1 in 5 didn't know he had a book, l.1693).
3. **Puddles, Ponds, Lakes, Oceans** — narrow your content niche first, then widen over time.
4. **Content creates tools for salespeople** — keep a "greatest hits" list labeled by problem/benefit.
5. **Free content retains paying customers** — buyers consume your free content and factor it into ROI.
6. **People don't have shorter attention spans, they have higher standards** — "too boring," not "too
   long."
7. **Avoid pre-scheduling posts** — manual posting's tight feedback loop makes you try harder.

### Benchmarks (l.1665–1733)

- Measure monthly: **total followers + reach** (how big) and **growth rate** (how fast, e.g. +500 on
  1,000 = 50%/mo) (l.1709–1725).
- **78% of clients had consumed ≥2 long-form pieces before booking a call** — free content nurtures the
  demand paid ads take credit for (l.1675).
- Patience benchmark: his podcast ran **twice a week for 4 years** before cracking the Top 100, and hit
  **Top 10 US** in year 5 (l.1729–1733).

### Output contract for `hormozi-lead-content`
Content units for *this* product with Hook (topic category + ≥2 headline components + platform format),
Retain (list/step/story structure), and Reward stated; the chosen give:ask cadence (integrated vs.
intermittent) with the filled-in ask/offer script; the scale approach (depth-then-width or reverse); and
the growth metrics to track.

## Cold Outreach

*(1-to-1 to a cold audience. Read by `hormozi-lead-cold`.)*

**How it works (l.1974–2018):** private one-to-one contact with strangers — the "more advanced cousin
of warm outreach," no longer capped by who you know. The one key difference: **trust — strangers don't
trust you** (l.1984). It's a **numbers game**: find how much outreach engages one lead, then do *more*.
Note the ramp is slow — the book's case study took ~a year (0 → 2 → 4 → 6 → 10 → 14 → 20 → 30
sales/month) before it printed (l.1938–1954).

### The 3 problems strangers create → the 3 steps that solve them (l.1988–2018)

Strangers mean: (1) you have no way to contact them, (2) they ignore you, (3) they're not interested.
Solve in this order: **1) Get a way to contact them → 2) Figure out what to say → 3) Contact them until
they're ready.**

**Step 1 — Build a list** (l.2020–2041). Work most-accessible → least:
1. **Software** — subscribe to scraping tools, search by criteria, test a few hundred, then pull all
   that match.
2. **Brokers** — pay list brokers to assemble to your criteria; test samples; keep who delivers.
3. **Elbow grease** — join groups/communities that hold your audience and scrape manually (slowest, but
   **freshest** — those people haven't been hit by everyone else, since anything searchable is already
   contacted). **Put your first 1,000 names together** (l.2038).

**Step 2 — Personalize, then give BIG FAST VALUE** (l.2042–2081). Two must-haves, because you have
seconds:
- **a) Personalize (act like you know them)** — make the *cold* reach out look *warm*: 1–3 facts a
  friend might know, a compliment, ideally how it benefited *you*. (The "dog-training" phone pattern,
  l.2052–2056: open with their name + a genuine reference to their content, *then* the pitch — never
  "wanna buy some marketing services?")
- **b) Big Fast Value** — "blow their minds in under thirty seconds" (l.2068); give away stuff people
  *actually pay for*, not a thinly-veiled sales call. (Swapping "game planning" — code for a sales call
  — for real free service **3×'d take rates** and turned cold outreach into a monster channel, l.2074.)
- Script lengths: phone/chat **never more than a page or two**; cold email **rarely more than half a
  page**; ship your first 100 conversations / 10,000 emails before tweaking (l.2080).

**Step 3 — Volume** (l.2082–2137). Make up for a lower response rate with reach:
- **a) Automate delivery** — record once, send to many (pre-recorded voicemail/voice memo, templated
  email/text, pre-recorded video) vs. manual (live script, handwritten letter).
- **b) Automate distribution** — robo-dialers, email/text/voicemail blasts. **You trade personalization
  for scale; the fewer leads you have, the less automation you should use** (personalize the 1,000
  hedge-fund managers; automate to tens of millions of dieters) (l.2100–2102). Allocate **10–20% of
  effort to new/untested tech** (l.2104).
- **c) Follow up — more times, more ways.** Most people don't. Different people respond to different
  channels; use non-response on one as the reason to try another ("*calling to follow up on my
  email*"). Expect **2–3 conversations before a higher-ticket sale** (l.2118). After finishing the
  list, **wait 3–6 months, then run it again** — they may not have seen it, the timing may have been
  wrong, or their circumstances changed (l.2124–2136).

### Benchmarks (l.2144–2163)

- **Phone:** 100 cold calls/day × **20% pickup** × **25% take the magnet** = **4 engaged leads**; over
  ~4 hours that's **~1 engaged lead/hour** (l.2152).
- **Email:** 100 personalized/day × **30% open** × **10% reply** = **3 engaged leads (3%)**; **shoot
  for ~3%** of the list becoming engaged leads (a sample campaign hit **4%**) (l.2156–2158).
- **DM (personal video/voice memo):** 100/day × **20% reply** = **20 engaged leads**, then qualify with
  A-C-A (l.2162).
- **Success bar:** make **at least 3× the lifetime profit of a customer vs. what it costs to get them**
  — the bare minimum; one portfolio company gets **30 : 1** (l.2152, l.2162).

### Costs — worked example (l.2168–2188)
Rep at **$15/hr + $50/show**; **$3,600 profit/sale**; leads **$0.10**; 200 leads/day → ~2 shows/day; an
8-hr shift = **$120 labor + $100 commissions + $20 leads = $240 for 2 shows = $120/show**; close 33% →
**$360 CAC**; against $3,600 profit that's a **10 : 1 return** (l.2186). Then "just add bodies."
Reliability equation (l.2200–2202): if 100 emails → 1 customer, then 100 customers → 10,000 emails =
333/day; at 111 emails/person/day that's **3 people**.

### Output contract for `hormozi-lead-cold`
The targeted list source + first-1,000 plan; the personalization research method; the **big-fast-value**
offer/magnet; the phone / email / DM scripts (personalize → big fast value → CTA); the volume + follow-up
cadence (times, ways, 3–6-month re-run); and the tracked funnel metrics against the 3:1 minimum.

## Paid Ads

*(1-to-many to a cold audience. Read by `hormozi-lead-paid`.)*

**How it works (l.2274–2287):** pay someone to put your offer in front of *their* cold audience —
"renting eyeballs or earballs." The fastest way to reach the most people; **reach is guaranteed, getting
your money back isn't**, so it's a **game of efficiency**, not reach. Start with a small profitable
"puddle" audience, then scale to pond→lake→ocean — efficiency drops as you widen, but total profit rises
(l.2286).

### The 4 problems → 4 steps (l.2288–2536)

**Step 1 — Find a platform** where four things are true (l.2298–2312): you've used it and gotten value
from it; you can target your people on it; you know how to format ads for it; you have the minimum money
to place an ad.

**Step 2 — Target them** (l.2314–2332): two methods, usable together — **lookalike audience** (upload
your best list — current/past customers first, then warm, then cold, to hit the platform minimum) +
**target with factors** (age, income, gender, interests, time, location). More filters = more efficient
but faster burn; small specific wins fund bigger broader audiences later — "this is how you scale."

**Step 3 — Build the ad: Call Out + Value + CTA** (l.2334–2523):
- **1) Call Out** — the most important part "by a lot"; focus the majority of effort on the **first five
  seconds** (it made his advertising ~**20× more effective**, l.2352). Harness the **cocktail-party
  effect** — specific enough to catch the right people, broad enough to catch many. **Verbal callouts:**
  **Labels** (group descriptors — "LOCAL AREA + TYPE OF PERSON" is a perennial winner), **Yes Questions**
  (self-qualifying), **If-Then Statements**, **Ridiculous Results** (l.2362–2377). **Nonverbal
  callouts:** **Contrast** (stands out), **Likeness** ("quack like a duck" — look/sound like the
  audience; mascots endure), **The Scene** (visually *show* the yes-question / if-then) (l.2380–2420).
- **2) Value — the What-Who-When framework** (l.2426–2506). **What = 8 key elements** = the 4 Value-
  Equation drivers + their 4 opposites: **Dream Outcome / Nightmare**, **Perceived Likelihood / Risk**,
  **Time Delay / Speed**, **Effort & Sacrifice / Ease** — show the carrot *and* the stick. **Who** =
  run each element through the customer *and* the people who give them status (spouse, kids, boss,
  rivals). **When** = run it across past / present / future. More angles = more interest (long vs. short
  ad = how many angles you cover; keep callout + CTA constant) (l.2498).
- **3) CTA — tell them exactly what to do next** (l.2510–2522): S-P-E-L-L it out (click this, call this,
  reply "YES," scan this). Keep it quick/easy (short memorable domains); layer on urgency/scarcity/
  bonuses from the lead-magnet CTA toolkit.

**Step 4 — Get permission to contact them** (l.2526–2536): a simple **landing page** (focus on words +
image). **Match the landing page to the ad** — one continuous experience "from click to close"; use
Cialdini consistency ("now that you did A, do B") to move them to give contact info. You're not selling
— you're asking if they're interested; when they hand over contact info they become an **engaged lead**.

### Money stuff — the Three Phases of Scaling Paid Ads (l.2570–2602)

- **Phase 1 — Track Money:** before spending a dollar, set up accurate tracking (consultant, tutorials).
  Without it "you're gonna get cleaned out"; with it you can do more of what works.
- **Phase 2 — Lose Money** ("investing in a money-printing machine"): you pay first, so the account dips
  before it rises. Expect to **lose more times than you win**, but cap the losses and scale the wins —
  e.g. $100 × 10 ads = $1,000; 9 lose, 1 returns $500 → then **100× down** on the winner: $10,000 →
  $50,000 (l.2588). **Test budget = 2× the cash you collect from a customer in 30 days** (not LTGP); if
  an ad gets *no* leads at all, kill it before 1× 30-day cash (l.2592–2594).
- **Phase 3 — Print Money:** once you make back more than you spend, **spend as much as you can**.
  Reverse the budget from your sales goal and **pad ~20%** for scaling inefficiency — e.g. want 100
  customers at $100 CAC = $10,000, +20% = **$12,000 / 30 days = $400/day** (l.2600–2602).

### Efficiency benchmarks — LTGP : CAC (l.2604–2634)

Measure **Lifetime Gross Profit (LTGP)** — all a customer ever spends minus all it costs to deliver —
against **Cost to Acquire a Customer (CAC)**. Profitable when LTGP > CAC. **Aim for at least 3 : 1**;
below 3:1, businesses struggle to scale — above it, they take off (a pattern, not a rule, l.2616).
Diagnose ads vs. business model with the **industry-average CAC**: if your CAC is **below 3× the
industry average**, fix the **business model** (raise LTGP); if **above 3×**, fix the **advertising**
(lower CAC) (l.2630). Costs approach zero but LTGP can rise to infinity — so eventually, just make more.

### Client-Financed Acquisition (CFA) — the fix when ads aren't profitable (l.2636–2678)

The problem: LTGP often exceeds CAC only *over months*, so first-purchase profit < CAC → a cash-flow
crunch that caps scale. **CFA:** if the customer pays you **more than the cost to get *and* fulfill them
in the first 30 days**, you can recycle the cash and scale now and forever (30 days = interest-free
credit-card float). *Worked example:* $15/mo membership − $5 cost = $10 GP/mo; 10-mo life = **$100
LTGP**; **$30 CAC** → **3.3 : 1** — profitable, but only $10 trickles in monthly. **Fix: immediately
sell more** — a **$100 upsell** at 100% margin taken by **1 in 5** adds **$20/customer**; $10 + $20 =
**$30 collected in 30 days = break-even = "free customers,"** with every later $10/mo as gravy. This is
how he scaled every company past **$1M/mo within 12 months without outside funding** (l.2676).

### Paid-ads lessons (l.2680–2690)
1. **Don't confuse a sales problem with an advertising problem** — if the right leads with money aren't
   buying, the ads work; the *sales* process is broken.
2. **Your best free content makes the best paid ads** — especially **User-Generated Content** (customer
   testimonials/reviews).
3. **If you say you suck at something (e.g. "I'm not techy"), you will** — it just keeps you poorer.

### Output contract for `hormozi-lead-paid`
The chosen platform (4 requirements met); the targeting plan (lookalike list order + factor filters);
the ad built as **Call Out (verbal/nonverbal) + Value (What-Who-When, 8 elements) + CTA**; the matched
landing page; the scaling plan across the Three Phases with the **test budget (2× 30-day cash)** and
**daily budget (goal ÷ CAC, +20%)**; and the **LTGP:CAC** target (≥3:1) plus a **CFA** plan (30-day
break-even via upsell) — all figures from real economics or `<placeholder>`.

**Warm Outreach:** how it works + 10 steps + A-C-A + Value-Equation offer script + free offer + "what if
they say no" + 9-word email + benchmarks (l.1003–1257). **Post Free Content:** Content Unit
Hook/Retain/Reward + topics/headlines/format + curiosity structures + give:ask + integrated/intermittent
asks + scaling + 7 lessons + benchmarks (l.1349–1733). **Cold Outreach:** trust + 3 problems/3 steps +
list-building + personalize/big-fast-value + volume/automation/follow-up + phone/email/DM benchmarks +
